idiom_name: typed watchdog state machine over a resettable timer with an injected Clock (AbortSignal.timeout for bounded probes)
implementation_notes: Same runtime primitives as JavaScript, but the alert state is expressed as a discriminated union (watching | silent | alerted) with an injected Clock interface, so debounce, repeat-while-silent and clear-on-arrival are exhaustive by construction and testable with a fake clock instead of real timers; AbortSignal.timeout(ms) bounds out-of-band probes (queue depth, health endpoints) without hand-managed timers. The classic watchman object reappears here only when many subjects must share one sweep, which is where the typed registry earns its keep; for a single subscription the resettable timer plus the union state is the whole implementation.
pitfalls: Declaring the clock as Date or number hides the wall-clock hazard: inject a Clock { now(): number } backed by performance.now() in production and a controllable fake in tests, or an NTP step silently produces negative silence.
setTimeout's handle type differs by lib/DOM setting (NodeJS.Timeout vs number): store ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> instead of number, or the same file fails to compile when the lib changes.

A discriminated union only pays off if every transition is handled: keep an assertNever in the default branch, otherwise the recovery path (alerted -> watching) is exactly the one that gets forgotten.
TypeScript's structural typing lets a Date sneak into a number slot if the clock is not branded - the branded Clock is what makes the monotonic requirement enforceable rather than a comment.
